Commenting Code and Best Practices for Code Maintenance
Introduction:
Writing clean, readable, and maintainable code is just as important as writing code that works. Good commenting and maintenance practices make your code more understandable to others (and your future self). Let’s dive into why and how we should comment our code and some best practices for code maintenance.

Part I: Understanding Code Commenting
1.1: What is Code Commenting?
Code commenting involves adding descriptive lines to your code to explain what certain parts of the code are intended to do. These lines are ignored by the compiler or interpreter.
1.2: Why is Commenting Important?
Comments improve the readability of your code by providing context. They can explain the purpose of a particular code block, provide additional information about a complex algorithm, or clarify a tricky section of code.

Part II: Best Practices for Commenting Code
2.1: Comment on the “Why”, not the “What”
Your comments should explain why the code does something, not what it does. If the code’s purpose is not immediately clear, consider refactoring it to make it more readable.
2.2: Keep Comments Concise
Comments should be brief and to the point. If you need a lengthy explanation to understand a piece of code, it may be a sign that you need to simplify or refactor your code.
2.3: Avoid Redundant Comments
Don’t write comments for code that is self-explanatory. For example, there’s no need to comment on a line of code that just increments a counter.
2.4: Update Comments as Code Changes
Make sure your comments always reflect the current state of your code. Outdated comments can lead to confusion and misinformation.

Part III: Importance of Code Maintenance
Maintaining code is about ensuring your code stays clean, understandable, and easy to debug over time. This includes commenting, but also involves practices like refactoring, using version control, and regularly reviewing code.

Part IV: Best Practices for Code Maintenance
4.1: Regular Refactoring
Refactoring involves changing the code’s structure without changing its functionality. Regular refactoring makes your code more efficient, readable, and maintainable.
4.2: Use Version Control Systems
Version control systems like Git help you track changes, understand how your codebase evolves over time, and make it easier to revert changes or branch out for testing new features.
4.3: Conduct Regular Code Reviews
Regularly reviewing your code and your team’s code can help spot potential issues before they become problems. Code reviews also promote knowledge sharing among team members.
4.4: Follow a Coding Standard
Adhere to a coding standard or style guide to keep your code consistent. This will make it easier for others (and yourself) to read and understand your code.
4.5: Write Unit Tests
Writing unit tests can help you catch bugs early, ensure that your code works as expected, and prevent future changes from breaking functionality.

Conclusion:
Commenting your code and maintaining it properly is crucial for long-term project success. Good practices help your future self and others understand your code better, make it easier to debug, and create a more collaborative environment. Remember that writing code is not just about getting a machine to perform tasks, but also about communicating your thought process effectively to other developers.

Introduction:
Docker and Kubernetes are two prominent tools used in deploying and managing applications in a modern development pipeline. Although they are often discussed together, they serve different, albeit complementary, roles. It’s crucial to understand the unique functions of Docker and Kubernetes and how they can work together.

Part I: Overview of Docker and Kubernetes
1.1: What is Docker?
Docker is an open-source platform that automates the deployment, scaling, and management of applications by encapsulating them into containers. A Docker container packages an application along with all of its dependencies, ensuring that it will run uniformly regardless of the host environment.
1.2: What is Kubernetes?
Kubernetes (also known as K8s) is an open-source platform for automating the deployment, scaling, and managing of containerized applications. It groups containers into “pods” (the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes) and manages these pods across multiple host machines.

Part II: Comparing Docker and Kubernetes
2.1: Scope
Docker focuses on automating application deployment within containers, ensuring consistency across environments. Kubernetes, on the other hand, manages clusters of containers across multiple machines, handling tasks like load balancing, network traffic distribution, and service discovery.
2.2: Scalability
While Docker can scale applications, its capacity is limited. Kubernetes excels at managing and scaling large clusters of containers, making it more suitable for large-scale applications.
2.3: Networking
In Docker, each container has its unique IP, with linking allowing containers to communicate. Kubernetes uses a flat network model, allowing all pods to communicate with each other without needing to map ports.
2.4: Data Storage
Docker volumes can be used for persistent data storage. Kubernetes, while also supporting Docker volumes, provides its volume abstraction layer, making it compatible with numerous cloud storage options.
2.5: Load Balancing
Docker uses a simple DNS-based round-robin method for load balancing. Kubernetes, however, provides more advanced load balancing features, including the distribution of network traffic to maintain stable application performance.

Part III: Docker and Kubernetes Working Together
Docker and Kubernetes are not mutually exclusive; instead, they complement each other. Docker provides the containerization technology, and Kubernetes provides orchestration capabilities for managing large clusters of Docker containers.

Part IV: When to Use Docker or Kubernetes
4.1: Use Docker When:

You are containerising applications and ensuring consistent behavior across environments.
Your application is relatively simple and does not require advanced orchestration or scaling features.
You want a simpler learning curve. Docker is generally easier to learn and implement.

4.2: Use Kubernetes When:

You need to manage and scale large clusters of containers across multiple machines.
Your application requires advanced orchestration features, such as load balancing, service discovery, and automated rollouts and rollbacks.
You are deploying microservices architecture at a large scale.


Conclusion:
Understanding Docker and Kubernetes and their respective strengths can help you make informed decisions when deploying and managing your applications. While Docker provides an excellent platform for containerising applications, Kubernetes offers powerful tools for managing and scaling those containers. Choosing the right tool depends on your specific use case, the complexity and scale of your application, and your infrastructure needs.

In today’s blog, I will discuss a pivotal concept in modern machine learning architectures: MLOps, short for Machine Learning Operations.


MLOps is a set of best practices combining Machine Learning (ML), Data Engineering, and DevOps. The goal of MLOps is to streamline and standardize the machine learning lifecycle, from development and deployment to maintenance.
MLOps aims to address various challenges in operationalizing ML models, such as managing data dependencies, maintaining code quality, ensuring model reproducibility, and monitoring model performance over time.



Let’s dive deeper into the various components that constitute MLOps:


Version control is essential for tracking changes to code, data, parameters, and environment configuration. Git is often used for code, but tools like DVC (Data Version Control) can help manage data and model versions.



Testing ensures the stability and reliability of the code, including model code and infrastructure code. Types of tests include unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests. Additionally, data validation tests are crucial to ensure the quality of the data feeding into the models.



CI is a practice where developers frequently merge their code changes into a central repository. After each merge, automated builds and tests are run. In the context of MLOps, this includes integration tests of ML code, infrastructure, and data pipelines.



Continuous Deployment is the practice of automatically deploying the code to production after passing the build and test stages. For ML, this also includes model training, validation, and deployment.



Model performance needs to be monitored over time to ensure it doesn’t degrade. Monitoring systems can track model performance metrics and provide alerts for any significant changes. Logging systems keep detailed records of data inputs and outputs, model predictions, and any errors or exceptions.



Ensuring the same results can be achieved if a past version of the model is re-run with the same data and parameters is key. This includes versioning data, code, and environment, as Ill as tracking all experiments.




Several tools and platforms help facilitate MLOps, including:

MLflow: An open-source platform for managing the end-to-end ML lifecycle, including experimentation, reproducibility, and deployment.
TFX (TensorFlow Extended): A Google-production-scale ML platform that provides a configuration framework and shared libraries to integrate common components needed to define, launch, and monitor ML systems.
Kubeflow: An open-source project dedicated to making deployments of machine learning workflows on Kubernetes simple, portable, and scalable.
Seldon: An open-source platform that enables businesses to deploy, scale, and optimize machine learning models in production.




MLOps brings several benefits, including:

Efficiency: By automating many steps in the ML lifecycle.
Reproducibility: By tracking every experiment with its data, code, and parameters.
Collaboration: By enabling data scientists, data engineers, and DevOps to work together effectively.
Monitoring: By continuously monitoring model performance and data quality.
Governance and regulatory compliance: By maintaining detailed logs of data, model predictions, and model changes.

The ultimate goal of MLOps is to accelerate the ML lifecycle and make ML models more valuable to the organization. Having a firm grasp of MLOps principles has been invaluable in my professional journey.

title: Dr Juan Beltran
text:
Following our introductory session on MLOps, today we will delve deeper into each component of the MLOps lifecycle and understand their practical applications.


The quality and consistency of data are critical for the performance of ML models. As such, versioning data is an important practice in MLOps. Tools like DVC can be used for this purpose. They keep track of changes in datasets and models, enabling you to reproduce any version of your experiment.
Also, don’t forget about data validation: tools like TensorFlow Data Validation (TFDV) can help you analyze and validate the consistency of your data over time.



During this stage, data scientists build and train various machine learning models to solve the given problem. Key aspects of this stage are tracking experiments and ensuring reproducibility. An experiment involves a specific version of the code, a set of parameters, a dataset, and produces a model and its metrics. MLflow is a popular tool used to manage these experiments.
To ensure reproducibility, you must have version control in place for not just your code (using Git), but also your data and model (using tools like DVC or MLflow). Containerization technologies (like Docker) can also be used to maintain the consistency of the computing environment across different stages of the ML lifecycle.



In MLOps, testing isn’t limited to just the code; it also involves data testing and model validation.

Data Tests: These tests ensure that the data is in the correct format, within the expected range, and not corrupted.
Model Tests: These tests confirm that the model is performing as expected and that its predictions make sense. Model validation techniques, like cross-validation or train/validation/test split, are used to assess the performance of the model.




CI/CD are key DevOps practices that have been adapted for MLOps.

Continuous Integration (CI): This involves regularly merging code changes into a central repository, after which automated builds and tests are run. CI ensures that the code remains in a deployable state and helps to catch bugs early.
Continuous Deployment (CD): In CD, code changes are automatically deployed to production once they pass the necessary automated tests. In the context of MLOps, CD often involves deploying ML models to a serving infrastructure, which could be a server, a serverless platform, or an edge device.

Tools like Jenkins, Travis CI, or GitLab CI/CD are often used for implementing CI/CD pipelines.



Once the model is deployed, it’s important to continuously monitor its performance to ensure that it’s still providing valuable predictions as new data comes in. This can be achieved using monitoring tools like Prometheus or Grafana. Logging systems like Elasticsearch or Fluentd can help store detailed records of data inputs and outputs, model predictions, and any errors or exceptions.



In many industries, there are regulations requiring that models be explainable, fair, and unbiased. Thus, MLOps also involves applying techniques for model interpretability (like SHAP or LIME), and ensuring data privacy (like differential privacy or federated learning). Furthermore, maintaining detailed logs and implementing proper access control mechanisms can help meet regulatory compliance requirements.
We’ll continue exploring these components in our hands-on session where we’ll walk through the lifecycle of an ML project using popular MLOps tools.

Following our detailed discussion on MLOps components, it’s now time to put theory into practice. Today’s session will focus on implementing an end-to-end machine learning project using the MLOps principles we’ve learned.
We will use a mix of tools for different stages of the project, including DVC for data versioning, MLflow for experiment tracking, Jenkins for CI/CD, and Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring.


Firstly, we’ll set up a collaborative environment with Git for version control. We will also set up DVC to track changes in our data and model files. All project members will clone the Git repository and set up DVC remotes.



In this step, we will prepare and explore the dataset. We’ll create scripts for data cleaning and preprocessing, ensuring we annotate them with proper comments for clarity. Once we have a processed dataset ready for ML modeling, we’ll use DVC to track the data file.



Next, we will start building and training our models. It’s important to track the hyperparameters, metrics, and models for each experiment. We’ll use MLflow for this purpose. MLflow will allow us to compare different experiments and choose the best model for our problem.



Now, we will create unit tests for our code, data validation tests for our dataset, and model validation tests for our model. For each code commit, these tests will run automatically in our Jenkins CI/CD pipeline.



Once we have a model that performs well and passes all tests, it’s time to deploy it. We’ll create a Docker image that includes our model and the necessary serving code, and we’ll configure Jenkins to deploy this image automatically to our serving infrastructure.



After deployment, we need to monitor the model’s performance in real-time. We will set up Prometheus to collect metrics from our model server, and we’ll use Grafana to create a dashboard for viewing these metrics.



MLOps is not a one-time setup; it’s a continuous process. We’ll set up alerts to inform us when our model’s performance drops below a certain threshold. If that happens, or if we receive new data, we’ll iterate on our models: we’ll go back to the experimentation stage, make improvements, and push the changes through our CI/CD pipeline.
Remember, MLOps is about managing the lifecycle of machine learning projects in a way that promotes collaboration, efficiency, and reliability. The tools and techniques we’re learning in this course will serve you well in your future data science endeavors.
In the next session, we’ll get hands-on with these tools, and you’ll have the opportunity to set up your own MLOps pipelines.

Neural Networks and Deep Learning Theory
Introduction:
Neural networks and deep learning have revolutionized numerous fields, including image recognition, natural language processing, and autonomous vehicles. This series of tutorial notes will provide a foundational understanding of these topics.

Part I: Introduction to Neural Networks
1.1: What is a Neural Network?
A neural network is a computing system inspired by the human brain’s neural network. It’s composed of interconnected processing nodes, called neurons or nodes. These nodes are organized in layers: an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer.
1.2: The Neuron
The basic computational unit of a neural network is the neuron. It receives input from other neurons, processes it, and sends its output to other neurons in the network. Each input is weighted, and these weights get adjusted during the learning process.
1.3: Activation Functions
An activation function defines the output of a neuron given a set of inputs. It transforms the weighted sum of the inputs into the output of the neuron. Common activation functions include sigmoid, ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit), and tanh.

Part II: The Learning Process in Neural Networks
2.1: Forward Propagation
During forward propagation, data flows from the input layer through the hidden layers to the output layer. Each neuron performs a weighted sum of inputs and passes the result through an activation function.
2.2: Backward Propagation (Backpropagation)
Backpropagation is a method to adjust the weights of the neurons based on the error of the network’s output. The network calculates the gradient of the loss function concerning each weight and adjusts the weights to minimize the loss.
2.3: Gradient Descent and Optimizers
Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that iteratively moves in the direction of steepest descent to minimize a function, in our case, the loss function. Optimizers like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Adam, RMSprop use different techniques to speed up this process.

Part III: Introduction to Deep Learning
3.1: What is Deep Learning?
Deep Learning is a subfield of machine learning concerned with algorithms inspired by the structure and function of the brain’s neural networks. It uses multiple layers of neural networks to model complex patterns in data.
3.2: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
CNNs are a type of deep learning model particularly effective for image recognition tasks. They employ a mathematical operation called convolution to process data from the image pixels.
3.3: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
RNNs are a class of neural networks for processing sequential data. LSTM is a type of RNN that can learn and remember over long sequences and is less likely to suffer from the vanishing gradient problem.

Part IV: Regularization, Overfitting, and Underfitting
4.1: Understanding Overfitting and Underfitting
Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too well, including noise and outliers, leading to poor generalization to new data. Underfitting is when the model does not learn enough from the training data, resulting in poor performance on both training and test data.
4.2: Regularization Techniques
Regularization helps prevent overfitting by adding a penalty to the loss function based on the complexity of the model. Techniques include L1 and L2 regularization, dropout, and early stopping.

Part V: Evaluation Metrics and Model Tuning
5.1: Loss Functions
Loss functions quantify how well the model’s predictions match the true values. Common loss functions include mean
squared error for regression tasks and cross-entropy for classification tasks.
5.2: Evaluation Metrics
Evaluation metrics help assess model performance. For classification tasks, these include accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. For regression tasks, common metrics include mean absolute error and root mean squared error.
5.3: Hyperparameter Tuning
Hyperparameters are the parameters of the learning process, not learned from the data. Tuning them can significantly improve model performance. Techniques include grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization.

Conclusion:
Neural networks and deep learning represent a vast and rapidly evolving field. Understanding the foundational theory and principles equips you with the ability to effectively apply these tools, continue learning about new developments, and even contribute to pushing the boundaries of what’s possible.

The Importance of Creating Environments in Python and Best Practices
Introduction:
When working on multiple Python projects, it’s essential to create separate environments to keep dependencies, libraries, and even Python versions isolated from one another. This practice ensures that our projects remain clean, manageable, and free from package conflict. It’s an industry-standard best practice that all Python developers, including data scientists, should follow.

Part I: Understanding Python Environments
1.1: What is a Python Environment?
A Python environment is a context in which you run Python code and includes everything that Python interacts with - the Python interpreter, libraries, and global settings.
1.2: Why Do We Need Python Environments?
Creating separate environments helps prevent conflicts between packages and Python versions when working on different projects. Each project can have its own dependencies, regardless of what dependencies other projects have.

Part II: Importance of Creating Python Environments
2.1: Isolation of Project Dependencies
By isolating your project environments, you avoid issues such as package version conflicts and the subsequent “dependency hell.” It ensures that upgrading a package for one project doesn’t break another.
2.2: Reproducibility
Environments help ensure that your code runs consistently across different platforms. By specifying the versions of packages used in an environment, you can ensure that your code will run the same way on any machine.
2.3: Ease of Sharing and Collaboration
When sharing your code with others, it is easier if you also provide the environment used to run it. This way, collaborators can replicate your environment and run your code without having to resolve any dependency issues.

Part III: Tools for Python Environment Management
3.1: Virtualenv
Virtualenv is a popular tool that creates isolated Python environments. It allows you to create an environment, install the necessary packages, and then activate and deactivate the environment as needed.
3.2: Conda
Conda is a package manager that also manages environments. It’s particularly popular in the data science world because it makes it easy to install packages that are hard to compile from source code, like NumPy or SciPy.
3.3: Pipenv
Pipenv combines the capabilities of pip and virtualenv into one tool, providing both package management and virtual environment support. It introduces a “lock file” to lock the environment’s exact dependencies, improving reproducibility.
3.4: Docker
Docker isn’t a Python-specific tool, but it’s worth mentioning. It encapsulates your application and its environment into a container, ensuring consistency across multiple development and release cycles.

Part IV: Best Practices for Creating Python Environments
4.1: One Project, One Environment
Create a new environment for each project to isolate its dependencies. This practice is essential to avoid conflicts between different project dependencies.
4.2: Document Dependencies
Always keep a record of your project’s dependencies. Tools like pip can generate a requirements.txt file, and conda can create an environment.yml file.
4.3: Use Version Control
Version control systems like git can help keep track of changes, not only in your code but also in your environment setup. They can help you trace back what changes in your environment might have caused your code to break.
4.4: Clean Up Regularly
Old, unused environments can take up space and create clutter. It’s good practice to remove any environments you’re no longer using.

Conclusion:
Creating and managing Python environments might seem like an extra step in the development process, but it is crucial for creating stable, reproducible, and conflict-free Python projects. By understanding the importance of Python environments and following the best practices,
you can improve your Python development workflow and make your life as a Python developer or data scientist significantly easier.

The Power of R and Python for Data Science
Introduction:
One of the most common discussions in the data science world revolves around the choice between Python and R. Both languages have unique strengths and they are powerful tools when used effectively. A proficient data scientist can and often does, use both in their toolkit. These languages are not mutually exclusive, and each language can be the perfect tool for specific tasks. It’s all about understanding their unique strengths and leveraging them accordingly.

Part I: Understanding Python and R
1.1: Overview of Python
Python is a general-purpose language noted for its simplicity and readability. This makes it a fantastic choice for beginners in programming and data science. Python’s robustness comes from its extensive libraries and packages, which cover almost every aspect of data science.
1.2: Overview of R
R is a statistical programming language that was specifically designed for data analysis, making it a go-to language for statisticians and researchers. It’s well-respected for its comprehensive statistical and graphical capabilities. R also has a wealth of packages for specialized scientific computation tasks.

Part II: Strengths of Python in Data Science
2.1: Machine Learning
Python’s major strength lies in machine learning. Libraries like scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch offer tools for predictive modeling, neural networks, natural language processing, and more.
2.2: General Programming & Scripting
Python shines in general-purpose programming tasks. This makes it perfect for building data pipelines, web scraping, automation, web development, and more.
2.3: Community & Learning Resources
Python boasts a larger user community than R, leading to more resources for learning and troubleshooting. Websites like Stack Overflow have a massive amount of content related to Python, making it easier for new data scientists to find help.

Part III: Strengths of R in Data Science
3.1: Statistical Analysis
R is unparalleled in its statistical analysis capabilities. It has a wide range of in-built functions for testing statistical hypotheses and conducting complex data analyses.
3.2: Data Visualization
Although Python has Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Plotly, R’s ggplot2 package is considered one of the most sophisticated data visualization tools. It has a high level of flexibility and enables detailed layering and thematic customization.
3.3: Reporting and Reproducible Research
With tools like R Markdown, Shiny, and Knitr, R excels at creating reports and interactive web applications, allowing others to reproduce your analysis with the original data and code.

Part IV: Python vs R: A Comparative Summary

Ease of Learning: Python’s syntax is straightforward, making it easier for beginners to learn. However, R has a steeper learning curve but provides more statistical power.
Data Handling Capabilities: Python is preferred for large datasets and big data analysis due to its speed and efficiency, while R is better suited for dataset manipulation and statistical modeling.
Visualization: Python has several good visualization libraries, but many data scientists agree that R’s ggplot2 offers superior control and complexity.
Machine Learning: Python has a better machine learning ecosystem, which includes libraries like TensorFlow and PyTorch. R also has machine learning libraries like caret and mlr, but they are less developed compared to Python’s ecosystem.
Community Support: Python has a wider community, resulting in faster package development and troubleshooting assistance. However, R has strong support in academia and research-oriented industries.
Job Market: Python is generally more in demand in the industry. However, R is favored in specific sectors like biostatistics, bioinformatics, and academic research.


Part V: The Convergence - Python and R in Data Science
One shouldn’t have to choose between Python and R; instead, the focus should be on learning to use both effectively. Many professionals use both languages in their work - Python for data manipulation and machine learning, and R for data analysis and visualization.
5.1: Tools for Interoperability
Tools like Jupyter notebooks, Rpy2, and reticulate make it possible to use both languages interchangeably in the same project.
5.2: Building a Polyglot Data Science Toolkit
Data scientists can and should develop a toolkit that takes advantage of the strengths of both languages. For example, you might use Python’s scikit-learn for machine learning, R’s ggplot2 for advanced visualizations, and Python’s pandas for data manipulation.

Conclusion:
The “Python vs. R” debate is less about choosing one over the other and more about understanding the strengths of each language and using them to your advantage. Both languages have a significant role to play in the data science landscape and knowing when to use each one is a skill every data scientist should cultivate.

title: Dr Juan Beltran
text:
Principles of Time Series Analysis – From Traditional Methods to Neural Networks (with Examples in Python and R)
Introduction:
Time series analysis is a statistical approach to analyze time-ordered data. It allows us to extract meaningful statistics and identify patterns to forecast future data points. We’ll start with traditional methods and move towards advanced techniques like neural networks, providing examples in Python and R.

Part I: Traditional Time Series Analysis Methods
1.1: Autoregressive (AR) Models
Autoregressive models forecast future values based on past values. It assumes that past values have a linear influence on future values.
# Python example using statsmodels
from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg
model = AutoReg(data, lags=1)
model_fit = model.fit()
# R example using forecast package
library(forecast)
fit <- auto.arima(data)
1.2: Moving Average (MA) Models
MA models use past forecast errors in a regression-like model. The dependence between an observation and an error in a previous time step is accounted for by this model.
# Python example using statsmodels
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
model = ARIMA(data, order=(0, 0, 1))
model_fit = model.fit()
# R example using forecast package
library(forecast)
fit <- auto.arima(data)
1.3: Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) Models
ARIMA combines autoregressive, differencing, and moving average elements. It’s a versatile model that can model a range of time series patterns.
# Python example using statsmodels
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
model = ARIMA(data, order=(1, 1, 1))
model_fit = model.fit()
# R example using forecast package
library(forecast)
fit <- auto.arima(data)

Part II: Advanced Time Series Analysis Methods
2.1: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)
RNNs can use their internal state (memory) to process sequences of inputs, which makes them ideal for time series forecasting.
# Python example using Keras
from keras.models import Sequential
from keras.layers import SimpleRNN

model = Sequential()
model.add(SimpleRNN(units=50, activation='relu', input_shape=(n_steps, n_features)))
model.add(Dense(1))
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='mse')
2.2: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
LSTM is a type of RNN that can learn long-term dependencies. They’re widely used for sequence prediction problems and have proven to be particularly effective.
# Python example using Keras
from keras.models import Sequential
from keras.layers import LSTM, Dense

model = Sequential()
model.add(LSTM(50, activation='relu', input_shape=(n_steps, n_features)))
model.add(Dense(1))
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='mse')

Part III: Evaluating Time Series Models
Regardless of the type of model, it’s critical to evaluate its performance. Two common metrics for time series models are the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE).
# Python example using sklearn
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
from math import sqrt

y_pred = model.predict(test_data)
MAE = mean_absolute_error(test_data, y_pred)
RMSE = sqrt(mean_squared_error(test_data, y_pred))

# R example using Metrics package
library(Metrics)
y_pred <- forecast(fit, h=length(test_data))
MAE = mae(test_data, y_pred$mean)
RMSE = rmse(test_data, y_pred$mean)

Conclusion:
Time series analysis is a complex field with a variety of methods ranging from traditional statistical models to advanced neural networks. The choice of method depends on the nature of the problem, the availability of data, and the level of accuracy required. Understanding the underlying principles of these methods is crucial in selecting the appropriate model and accurately interpreting its results.

title: Tutorials
text:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a subfield of machine learning that focuses on how an agent ought to take actions in an environment to maximize some notion of cumulative reward. In this tutorial, we will go over the fundamental principles of RL and how to implement them in Python and R.


RL revolves around these main concepts:

Agent: The RL algorithm that learns from trial and error.
Environment: The context where the agent operates.
State: The current situation of the agent.
Action: All possible moves the agent can make.
Reward: Feedback from the environment.

The agent learns by interacting with its environment, it takes actions, the environment returns the new state and gives a reward. The goal of the agent is to maximize the sum of rewards.



One of the simplest ways to understand reinforcement learning is through Q-Learning. The objective of Q-Learning is to find a policy that is optimal in the sense that the expected value of the total reward over all successive steps is maximized.
The Q-Learning algorithm uses a table (Q-table) where we have a row for each state (s) and a column for each action (a). The cell at the intersection of state (s) and action (a) represents the expected future reward that the agent will get if it takes action (a) while in state (s).
Let’s start with the Python implementation of Q-learning.



For our Python implementation, we will use the OpenAI Gym environment, which provides different game scenarios for training reinforcement learning agents. We’ll work with the FrozenLake-v0 game.
import numpy as np
import gym
import random
import time
from IPython.display import clear_output

# Create the environment
env = gym.make("FrozenLake-v0")

# Initialize Q-table with zero
q_table = np.zeros([env.observation_space.n, env.action_space.n])

# Hyperparameters
num_episodes = 10000
max_steps_per_episode = 100

learning_rate = 0.1
discount_rate = 0.99

exploration_rate = 1
max_exploration_rate = 1
min_exploration_rate = 0.01
exploration_decay_rate = 0.001

rewards_all_episodes = []

# Q-learning algorithm
for episode in range(num_episodes):
    state = env.reset()

    done = False
    rewards_current_episode = 0

    for step in range(max_steps_per_episode): 
        exploration_rate_threshold = random.uniform(0, 1)
        if exploration_rate_threshold > exploration_rate:
            action = np.argmax(q_table[state,:]) 
        else:
            action = env.action_space.sample()

        new_state, reward, done, info = env.step(action)

        # Update Q-table for Q(s,a)
        q_table[state, action] = q_table[state, action] * (1 - learning_rate) + \
            learning_rate * (reward + discount_rate * np.max(q_table[new_state, :]))

        state = new_state
        rewards_current_episode += reward 

        if done == True: 
            break

    # Exploration rate decay
    exploration_rate = min_exploration_rate + \
        (max_exploration_rate - min_exploration_rate) * np.exp(-exploration_decay_rate*episode)

    rewards_all_episodes.append(rewards_current_episode)
This code creates an agent that learns to play
the FrozenLake-v0 game. The agent uses Q-Learning to learn how to play.



Now let’s implement the same Q-Learning in R. We’re going to make a simple grid world with four cells, where the agent needs to find the terminal state to get a reward.
library(MDPtoolbox)

# Define transition and reward matrices
S <- 4
A <- 2
T <- array(0, c(S, A, S))
R <- matrix(0, S, A)

# Define transitions
T[1, 1, 2] <- 1
T[2, 1, 3] <- 1
T[3, 1, 4] <- 1
T[4, 1, 4] <- 1

T[1, 2, 1] <- 1
T[2, 2, 1] <- 1
T[3, 2, 2] <- 1
T[4, 2, 3] <- 1

# Define rewards
R[3, 1] <- 1
R[4, 1] <- 1

# Run Q-Learning
result <- mdp_example_qlearning(T, R, 0.9, 10000)
The code above creates a simple environment using the MDPtoolbox library. The environment is a simple four-state system where the agent learns to navigate to the terminal state using Q-Learning.



Reinforcement learning is a powerful approach for tasks that involve sequential decision-making. This tutorial presented the fundamental concepts of RL and walked through an example of how to implement Q-Learning, a simple but powerful RL algorithm, in Python and R. Remember that the RL field is vast and complex, this is just the tip of the iceberg!
This tutorial is intended as a starting point. I encourage you to continue exploring more complex environments, policies, and algorithms as you continue your journey in reinforcement learning. Happy learning!

1. Setting up
SQLite needs no server. In Python it comes built in:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect("softs.db")
cur = con.cursor()
You can also use the command line (sqlite3 softs.db) or a GUI such as DB Browser for SQLite. Every SQL block below can be run with cur.execute("""...""").

title: SQL 101: Building a Softs Market Database
text:
2. Designing the tables
We will keep three tables:

contracts: one row per futures market (what it is, where it trades, its unit).
prices: daily settlement prices.
exports: monthly exports by origin country.

CREATE TABLE contracts (
    symbol      TEXT PRIMARY KEY,   -- e.g. 'CC'
    commodity   TEXT NOT NULL,      -- 'Cocoa'
    exchange    TEXT NOT NULL,      -- 'ICE US'
    unit        TEXT NOT NULL       -- 'USD/tonne'
);

CREATE TABLE prices (
    symbol      TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES contracts(symbol),
    date        DATE NOT NULL,
    settle      REAL NOT NULL,
    volume      INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (symbol, date)
);

CREATE TABLE exports (
    origin      TEXT NOT NULL,      -- 'Côte d''Ivoire'
    commodity   TEXT NOT NULL,
    month       DATE NOT NULL,      -- first day of the month
    tonnes      REAL NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (origin, commodity, month)
);
The composite primary keys stop you loading the same day or month twice, which is the most common data bug on a research desk.

title: SQL 101: Building a Softs Market Database
text:
3. Inserting data
INSERT INTO contracts VALUES
  ('CC', 'Cocoa',          'ICE US', 'USD/tonne'),
  ('KC', 'Coffee Arabica', 'ICE US', 'USc/lb'),
  ('SB', 'Sugar No.11',    'ICE US', 'USc/lb'),
  ('CT', 'Cotton No.2',    'ICE US', 'USc/lb');
In practice you load prices in bulk. A quick way to get continuous front-month prices for learning purposes is yfinance, then push the DataFrame into SQLite with pandas:
import yfinance as yf

tickers = {"CC": "CC=F", "KC": "KC=F", "SB": "SB=F", "CT": "CT=F"}
frames = []
for sym, tk in tickers.items():
    df = yf.download(tk, start="2015-01-01", end="2024-06-30")[["Close", "Volume"]]
    df = df.reset_index().rename(columns={"Date": "date", "Close": "settle", "Volume": "volume"})
    df["symbol"] = sym
    frames.append(df)

import pandas as pd
prices = pd.concat(frames)
prices.to_sql("prices", con, if_exists="append", index=False)
Continuous front-month series jump at every roll, so treat them as illustrative. For real analysis you would store individual contract months (e.g. CCN24) and build your own roll-adjusted series.
For exports, national statistics, the ICCO and the ICO publish monthly or quarterly figures; load them the same way with to_sql.

title: SQL 101: Building a Softs Market Database
text:
4. Querying
The latest cocoa prices:
SELECT date, settle
FROM prices
WHERE symbol = 'CC'
ORDER BY date DESC
LIMIT 10;
Filtering with conditions: every day in 2024 when cocoa settled above $10,000/t (it did, for the first time ever, in the spring of 2024):
SELECT date, settle
FROM prices
WHERE symbol = 'CC'
  AND date >= '2024-01-01'
  AND settle > 10000;

title: SQL 101: Building a Softs Market Database
text:
5. Aggregating
Average yearly price and volume per market:
SELECT symbol,
       strftime('%Y', date)  AS year,
       ROUND(AVG(settle), 2) AS avg_settle,
       SUM(volume)           AS total_volume
FROM prices
GROUP BY symbol, year
ORDER BY symbol, year;
HAVING filters after aggregation. Years in which arabica averaged above 200 USc/lb:
SELECT strftime('%Y', date) AS year, AVG(settle) AS avg_settle
FROM prices
WHERE symbol = 'KC'
GROUP BY year
HAVING AVG(settle) > 200;

title: SQL 101: Building a Softs Market Database
text:
6. Joining tables
Joins let you put context next to the numbers:
SELECT c.commodity, c.unit, p.date, p.settle
FROM prices p
JOIN contracts c ON c.symbol = p.symbol
WHERE p.date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM prices);
Total cocoa exports by origin for the 2022/23 season (October to September):
SELECT origin, ROUND(SUM(tonnes) / 1000, 1) AS kt
FROM exports
WHERE commodity = 'Cocoa'
  AND month BETWEEN '2022-10-01' AND '2023-09-01'
GROUP BY origin
ORDER BY kt DESC;
Note that softs run on crop years, not calendar years: cocoa and coffee seasons usually start in October. Getting the season boundaries right is half the job.

title: SQL 101: Building a Softs Market Database
SQL 101: Building a Softs Market Database

Next steps
In Advanced SQL we use window functions to compute moving averages, calendar spreads and year-on-year export changes directly in the database.

title: Advanced SQL: Market Analytics in the Database
text:
1. Window functions: moving averages
A 20-day and 100-day moving average for cocoa:
SELECT date,
       settle,
       AVG(settle) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 19 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)  AS ma20,
       AVG(settle) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 99 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)  AS ma100
FROM prices
WHERE symbol = 'CC'
ORDER BY date;
PARTITION BY runs the same calculation separately for each market:
SELECT symbol, date, settle,
       AVG(settle) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY date
                         ROWS BETWEEN 19 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma20
FROM prices;

title: Advanced SQL: Market Analytics in the Database
text:
2. Returns and volatility with LAG
WITH r AS (
  SELECT symbol, date, settle,
         LN(settle / LAG(settle) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY date)) AS log_ret
  FROM prices
)
SELECT symbol, strftime('%Y', date) AS year,
       ROUND(SQRT(252) * SQRT(AVG(log_ret * log_ret) - AVG(log_ret) * AVG(log_ret)), 3) AS ann_vol
FROM r
WHERE log_ret IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY symbol, year
ORDER BY symbol, year;
(SQLite needs its math extension for LN and SQRT; recent Python builds include it.) Run this and the 2024 cocoa row stands out: the 2023/24 rally came with volatility far above anything in the previous decade.

title: Advanced SQL: Market Analytics in the Database
section: 3. Common table expressions for readable logic
text:
3. Common table expressions for readable logic
CTEs (WITH ...) break long queries into named steps. Here we flag days when cocoa moved more than three rolling standard deviations, a simple anomaly alert:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT date, settle,
         settle / LAG(settle) OVER (ORDER BY date) - 1 AS ret
  FROM prices WHERE symbol = 'CC'
),
s AS (
  SELECT date, settle, ret,
         AVG(ret) OVER w AS mu,
         SQRT(AVG(ret * ret) OVER w - AVG(ret) OVER w * AVG(ret) OVER w) AS sd
  FROM r
  WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 60 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)
)
SELECT date, settle, ROUND(ret * 100, 2) AS pct_move
FROM s
WHERE ABS(ret - mu) > 3 * sd
ORDER BY date DESC;
Note the window ends at 1 PRECEDING, so today’s move is compared with history only. Letting today leak into its own baseline is a classic mistake.

title: Advanced SQL: Market Analytics in the Database
text:
4. Calendar spreads
If you store individual contract months (a contract column such as CCN24, CCU24), you can compute spreads with a self-join:
SELECT a.date,
       a.settle AS jul,
       b.settle AS sep,
       a.settle - b.settle AS jul_sep_spread
FROM futures a
JOIN futures b ON a.date = b.date
WHERE a.contract = 'CCN24'
  AND b.contract = 'CCU24'
ORDER BY a.date;
A wide positive spread (backwardation) usually signals tight nearby supply, which is exactly what the cocoa curve showed through 2024.

title: Advanced SQL: Market Analytics in the Database
text:
5. Seasonal comparisons
Exports this season versus last season, month by month:
WITH s AS (
  SELECT origin, month, tonnes,
         CASE WHEN CAST(strftime('%m', month) AS INT) >= 10
              THEN CAST(strftime('%Y', month) AS INT)
              ELSE CAST(strftime('%Y', month) AS INT) - 1 END AS season_start
  FROM exports
  WHERE commodity = 'Cocoa'
)
SELECT cur.origin, cur.month, cur.tonnes,
       prev.tonnes AS last_season,
       ROUND(100.0 * (cur.tonnes - prev.tonnes) / prev.tonnes, 1) AS pct_change
FROM s cur
LEFT JOIN s prev
  ON prev.origin = cur.origin
 AND prev.month  = date(cur.month, '-1 year')
WHERE cur.season_start = 2023
ORDER BY cur.origin, cur.month;
Cumulative season-to-date totals with a running sum (reusing the same s CTE):
-- WITH s AS (...) as above
SELECT origin, month,
       SUM(tonnes) OVER (PARTITION BY origin, season_start ORDER BY month) AS season_to_date
FROM s;

title: Advanced SQL: Market Analytics in the Database
text:
6. Ranking
Top three origins per commodity by exports in a season:
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT commodity, origin, SUM(tonnes) AS total,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY commodity ORDER BY SUM(tonnes) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM exports
  WHERE month BETWEEN '2022-10-01' AND '2023-09-01'
  GROUP BY commodity, origin
)
WHERE rnk <= 3;

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
1. Setting up
!pip install yfinance pandas numpy scikit-learn matplotlib
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
2. Getting the data
We use weekly front-month futures and currency prices from Yahoo Finance: sugar (SB=F), WTI crude (CL=F), USD/BRL (BRL=X) and the US dollar index (DX-Y.NYB).
tickers = {"sugar": "SB=F", "crude": "CL=F", "usdbrl": "BRL=X", "dxy": "DX-Y.NYB"}
raw = yf.download(list(tickers.values()), start="2010-01-01", end="2024-06-30", interval="1wk")["Close"]
raw = raw.rename(columns={v: k for k, v in tickers.items()}).dropna()
raw.tail()

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
3. Levels or returns?
Regressing one price level on another almost always gives an impressive R² that means nothing: both series trend, so they look related even when they are not (a “spurious regression”). The safer approach is to model weekly percentage changes.
rets = np.log(raw).diff().dropna()
rets.corr().round(2)
You should see a negative correlation between sugar and USD/BRL, and a positive one between sugar and crude, in line with the story above.

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
section: 4. Train and test split, in time order
text:
4. Train and test split, in time order
Never shuffle time series. Train on the past, test on the most recent data:
X = rets[["crude", "usdbrl", "dxy"]]
y = rets["sugar"]

split = int(len(rets) * 0.8)
X_train, X_test = X.iloc[:split], X.iloc[split:]
y_train, y_test = y.iloc[:split], y.iloc[split:]

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)          # fit on training data only
X_train_s, X_test_s = scaler.transform(X_train), scaler.transform(X_test)

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
5. Ordinary least squares
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error

ols = LinearRegression().fit(X_train_s, y_train)
pred = ols.predict(X_test_s)

print(dict(zip(X.columns, ols.coef_.round(4))))
print("Test R2:", round(r2_score(y_test, pred), 3))
For proper inference (standard errors, p-values) use statsmodels:
import statsmodels.api as sm
model = sm.OLS(y_train, sm.add_constant(X_train)).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})
print(model.summary())
The HAC option corrects the standard errors for autocorrelation, which weekly commodity returns usually have.
Reading the result. These are contemporaneous relationships: they explain how sugar moves alongside the real and oil in the same week. They do not forecast next week. That is a useful distinction when someone shows you a model with a high R².

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
6. Lasso, Ridge and Elastic Net
Regularisation shrinks coefficients to fight overfitting, which matters as soon as you add many correlated drivers (other currencies, freight, fertiliser prices, weather indices).
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, Ridge, ElasticNet

for name, m in {"Lasso": Lasso(alpha=0.001),
                "Ridge": Ridge(alpha=1.0),
                "ElasticNet": ElasticNet(alpha=0.001, l1_ratio=0.5)}.items():
    m.fit(X_train_s, y_train)
    print(name, dict(zip(X.columns, m.coef_.round(4))),
          "R2:", round(r2_score(y_test, m.predict(X_test_s)), 3))
Lasso can set weak drivers exactly to zero, which makes it a handy first filter when you have dozens of candidate variables.

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
7. A decision tree
Trees capture non-linear effects, such as the ethanol link only mattering when oil is high enough for ethanol parity to bind.
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=30).fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Tree R2:", round(r2_score(y_test, tree.predict(X_test)), 3))
A shallow tree usually does no better than the linear model here, which is itself a finding: these macro relationships are close to linear in returns.

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
8. Checking stability
Relationships change. A rolling regression shows whether the real and oil still matter as much as they used to:
from statsmodels.regression.rolling import RollingOLS
roll = RollingOLS(rets["sugar"], sm.add_constant(rets[["crude", "usdbrl"]]), window=104).fit()
roll.params[["crude", "usdbrl"]].plot(title="Two-year rolling betas for sugar")
plt.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8)
plt.show()
If the betas drift, a model trained on 2015 to 2020 can mislead you in 2024. Policy shocks such as India’s export restrictions in 2023 are exactly the kind of event that a macro regression cannot see.

title: Regression 101: What Drives Sugar Prices?
text:
Next steps
In Hyperparameters in regression P1 we tune these models properly, using cross-validation that respects time order.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 1: Tuning Without Look-Ahead
text:
1. What is a hyperparameter?
A hyperparameter is set before training rather than learned from the data. In Lasso and Ridge, alpha controls how hard coefficients are pushed towards zero. Too small and the model overfits noise; too large and it ignores real drivers.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 1: Tuning Without Look-Ahead
text:
2. Why ordinary cross-validation leaks
KFold(shuffle=True) mixes weeks from 2023 into the training set and then tests on 2016. The model has effectively seen the future. In markets this makes every model look better than it will ever be in live use.
The fix is TimeSeriesSplit, which always trains on the past and validates on the period that follows:
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=1)   # gap avoids overlap at the boundary

for i, (tr, va) in enumerate(tscv.split(X_train)):
    print(i, X_train.index[tr[0]].date(), "to", X_train.index[tr[-1]].date(),
          "| validate", X_train.index[va[0]].date(), "to", X_train.index[va[-1]].date())

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 1: Tuning Without Look-Ahead
text:
3. Grid search with a pipeline
Put the scaler inside a pipeline so it is refitted on each training fold. Scaling on the full sample is another quiet source of leakage.
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
import numpy as np

pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("model", Lasso(max_iter=10000))])

grid = GridSearchCV(
    pipe,
    param_grid={"model__alpha": np.logspace(-5, -1, 20)},
    cv=tscv,
    scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error",
)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("Best alpha:", grid.best_params_)
print("CV MAE:", -grid.best_score_)

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 1: Tuning Without Look-Ahead
text:
4. Randomised search
When there are several hyperparameters, sampling is faster than an exhaustive grid. Elastic Net has two:
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import loguniform, uniform

pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("model", ElasticNet(max_iter=10000))])

rand = RandomizedSearchCV(
    pipe,
    param_distributions={"model__alpha": loguniform(1e-5, 1e-1),
                         "model__l1_ratio": uniform(0, 1)},
    n_iter=50, cv=tscv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error", random_state=42,
)
rand.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(rand.best_params_)

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 1: Tuning Without Look-Ahead
text:
5. Final check on untouched data
Only after tuning do we look at the test period, once:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
best = rand.best_estimator_
print("Test MAE:", mean_absolute_error(y_test, best.predict(X_test)))
If test performance is much worse than cross-validated performance, the relationship has probably shifted, or the model was overfit. Both are common in softs, where regimes change with weather, policy and positioning.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 1: Tuning Without Look-Ahead
text:
6. Practical tips

Choose the metric that matches the use: MAE for typical error, directional accuracy if you care about the sign.
Prefer simple models when cross-validated scores are close; they hold up better out of sample.
Re-tune on a schedule (for example each quarter) rather than after every bad week.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 1: Tuning Without Look-Ahead

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa
section: 1. Why cocoa and why El Niño?
text:
1. Why cocoa and why El Niño?
Around 60% of the world’s cocoa comes from Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana. El Niño years tend to bring drier, hotter conditions to West Africa, and the strong 2023/24 El Niño coincided with poor crops, disease (swollen shoot) and the record rally of early 2024. The Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) is a free, monthly measure of El Niño, so it makes a natural candidate feature.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa
text:
2. Data

Cocoa prices: World Bank “Pink Sheet” monthly commodity prices (CMO-Historical-Data-Monthly.xlsx, free from the World Bank Commodity Markets page).
ONI: NOAA Climate Prediction Center, oni.ascii.txt.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# World Bank Pink Sheet (download the file first)
wb = pd.read_excel("CMO-Historical-Data-Monthly.xlsx", sheet_name="Monthly Prices", skiprows=4)
wb = wb.rename(columns={wb.columns[0]: "month"})
wb = wb[wb["month"].astype(str).str.match(r"^\d{4}M\d{2}$")]
wb["month"] = pd.to_datetime(wb["month"].str.replace("M", "-"), format="%Y-%m")
cocoa = wb.set_index("month")["Cocoa"].astype(float)

# NOAA ONI: three-month seasons, value assigned to the centre month
oni = pd.read_csv("https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/data/indices/oni.ascii.txt", sep=r"\s+")
season_to_month = {"DJF": 1, "JFM": 2, "FMA": 3, "MAM": 4, "AMJ": 5, "MJJ": 6,
                   "JJA": 7, "JAS": 8, "ASO": 9, "SON": 10, "OND": 11, "NDJ": 12}
oni["month"] = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=oni["YR"], month=oni["SEAS"].map(season_to_month), day=1))
oni = oni.set_index("month")["ANOM"]

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa
text:
3. Features without look-ahead
df = pd.DataFrame({"cocoa": cocoa, "oni": oni}).dropna()
df["ret"] = np.log(df["cocoa"]).diff()

feats = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
for lag in (1, 3, 6):
    feats[f"oni_lag{lag}"] = df["oni"].shift(lag)      # ONI is published with a delay
feats["mom_3m"]  = df["ret"].rolling(3).sum().shift(1)
feats["mom_12m"] = df["ret"].rolling(12).sum().shift(1)
feats["vol_6m"]  = df["ret"].rolling(6).std().shift(1)

target = df["ret"].shift(-1)          # next month's return
data = feats.join(target.rename("y")).dropna()

train = data.loc[:"2019-12"]
test  = data.loc["2020-01":]
X_train, y_train = train.drop(columns="y"), train["y"]
X_test,  y_test  = test.drop(columns="y"),  test["y"]
Every feature uses only information available before the month we predict. Getting this right matters far more than the choice of model.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa
text:
4. The objective function
Hyperopt minimises a function. We return time-series cross-validated error for a gradient boosting model:
from hyperopt import fmin, tpe, hp, Trials, STATUS_OK
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

def objective(params):
    model = GradientBoostingRegressor(
        n_estimators=int(params["n_estimators"]),
        max_depth=int(params["max_depth"]),
        learning_rate=params["learning_rate"],
        subsample=params["subsample"],
        random_state=0,
    )
    mae = -cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=tscv,
                           scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()
    return {"loss": mae, "status": STATUS_OK}

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa
text:
5. The search space
space = {
    "n_estimators":  hp.quniform("n_estimators", 50, 500, 25),
    "max_depth":     hp.quniform("max_depth", 1, 4, 1),
    "learning_rate": hp.loguniform("learning_rate", np.log(0.005), np.log(0.2)),
    "subsample":     hp.uniform("subsample", 0.5, 1.0),
}

trials = Trials()
best = fmin(objective, space, algo=tpe.suggest, max_evals=100, trials=trials,
            rstate=np.random.default_rng(42))
print(best)
Shallow trees (depth 1 or 2) usually win on monthly commodity data, because there are only a few hundred observations.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa
text:
6. Compare with a naive benchmark
Always compare a forecast with something simple. For returns, the honest benchmark is zero (no change):
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

final = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=int(best["n_estimators"]),
                                  max_depth=int(best["max_depth"]),
                                  learning_rate=best["learning_rate"],
                                  subsample=best["subsample"], random_state=0)
final.fit(X_train, y_train)

pred = final.predict(X_test)
print("Model MAE:", mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred))
print("Zero MAE: ", mean_absolute_error(y_test, np.zeros_like(y_test)))
print("Hit rate: ", (np.sign(pred) == np.sign(y_test)).mean())
Expect the model to struggle in the test period: 2023/24 was outside anything in the training data. That is the real lesson. Weather indices can help, but supply shocks of this size are why fundamental analysis (crop surveys, arrivals, grindings, disease) matters alongside models.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa
text:
7. Looking inside the trials
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
losses = [t["result"]["loss"] for t in trials.trials]
plt.plot(np.minimum.accumulate(losses))
plt.xlabel("Trial"); plt.ylabel("Best CV MAE so far")
plt.show()
If the curve flattens after 30 trials, extra evaluations are not buying you anything.

title: Hyperparameters in Regression, Part 2: Bayesian Optimisation on Cocoa

Next steps

title: Random Forest 101: Predicting Coffee’s Weekly Direction
text:
1. Data

Prices: weekly front-month arabica from Yahoo Finance (KC=F).
Positioning: the CFTC Commitments of Traders (COT) disaggregated report, which splits open interest into producers, swap dealers and managed money (funds). Funds’ net position is widely watched in softs because crowded positions can unwind sharply.

import io, zipfile, requests
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf

px = yf.download("KC=F", start="2012-01-01", end="2024-06-30", interval="1wk")["Close"].squeeze()

def load_cot(year):
    url = f"https://www.cftc.gov/files/dea/history/fut_disagg_txt_{year}.zip"
    z = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(requests.get(url).content))
    return pd.read_csv(z.open(z.namelist()[0]), low_memory=False)

cot = pd.concat(load_cot(y) for y in range(2012, 2025))
cot = cot[cot["Market_and_Exchange_Names"].str.startswith("COFFEE C")]
cot["date"] = pd.to_datetime(cot["Report_Date_as_YYYY-MM-DD"])
cot = cot.set_index("date").sort_index()
cot["mm_net_pct_oi"] = (cot["M_Money_Positions_Long_All"] - cot["M_Money_Positions_Short_All"]) / cot["Open_Interest_All"]
COT data are as of Tuesday but published on Friday, so we lag them by one week before use. Ignoring publication lags is one of the easiest ways to fool yourself.

title: Random Forest 101: Predicting Coffee’s Weekly Direction
text:
2. Features
df = pd.DataFrame({"px": px})
df["ret"] = np.log(df["px"]).diff()

X = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
X["ret_1w"]  = df["ret"]
X["ret_4w"]  = df["ret"].rolling(4).sum()
X["ret_13w"] = df["ret"].rolling(13).sum()
X["vol_13w"] = df["ret"].rolling(13).std()
X["dist_ma26"] = df["px"] / df["px"].rolling(26).mean() - 1
X["week_of_year"] = df.index.isocalendar().week.astype(int)   # Brazil harvest / frost seasonality

cot_w = cot["mm_net_pct_oi"].resample("W-SUN").last().shift(1)  # publication lag
X = X.join(cot_w.rename("mm_net")).ffill()
X["mm_net_chg_4w"] = X["mm_net"].diff(4)

y = (df["ret"].shift(-1) > 0).astype(int)   # 1 if next week is up
data = X.join(y.rename("up")).dropna()
The week-of-year feature lets the forest pick up seasonality: the Brazilian harvest from roughly May to September, and the frost-risk window in June to August that has driven some of arabica’s biggest rallies.

title: Random Forest 101: Predicting Coffee’s Weekly Direction
text:
3. Training, in time order
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report

train = data.loc[:"2020-12"]
test  = data.loc["2021-01":]
X_train, y_train = train.drop(columns="up"), train["up"]
X_test,  y_test  = test.drop(columns="up"),  test["up"]

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=20,
                            random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

pred = rf.predict(X_test)
print("Accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(y_test, pred), 3))
print("Base rate (always up):", round(y_test.mean(), 3))
print(classification_report(y_test, pred))
Compare accuracy with the base rate. In a trending market, “always up” can look like 55% accuracy without any skill.

title: Random Forest 101: Predicting Coffee’s Weekly Direction
text:
4. Tuning with time-series cross-validation
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, TimeSeriesSplit

grid = GridSearchCV(
    RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    {"n_estimators": [300, 600], "max_depth": [3, 4, 6], "min_samples_leaf": [10, 20, 40]},
    cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5), scoring="roc_auc",
)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(grid.best_params_, round(grid.best_score_, 3))
We score with ROC AUC, which judges how well the model ranks up-weeks above down-weeks, regardless of the 50% threshold.

title: Random Forest 101: Predicting Coffee’s Weekly Direction
text:
5. What did the forest learn?
Built-in feature importances are biased towards continuous variables. Permutation importance on the test set is more honest:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
imp = permutation_importance(grid.best_estimator_, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc",
                             n_repeats=20, random_state=0)
pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=X_test.columns).sort_values().plot.barh()
Positioning features often matter most at extremes: when funds are very long, the downside risk from liquidation rises.

title: Random Forest 101: Predicting Coffee’s Weekly Direction
text:
6. From probabilities to decisions
Instead of trading every week, act only when the model is confident:
proba = grid.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
signal = np.where(proba > 0.6, 1, np.where(proba < 0.4, -1, 0))
strategy = signal * df["ret"].shift(-1).reindex(X_test.index)
print("Weeks active:", (signal != 0).mean().round(2))
print("Cumulative log return:", strategy.sum().round(3))
This ignores costs, rolls and slippage, so treat it as a sanity check rather than a backtest.

title: Random Forest 101: Predicting Coffee’s Weekly Direction

XGBoost 101 applies gradient boosting to cocoa and adds weather signals.

title: XGBoost 101: Cocoa, Weather and the Curve
text:
1. Data

Cocoa prices: World Bank Pink Sheet monthly prices (see Part 2 of the regression tutorials for loading code).
Rainfall: CHIRPS monthly precipitation, averaged over the cocoa belt of Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana. You can export it from Google Earth Engine with the script in the Google Earth Engine tutorial, as a CSV with columns month and rain_mm.
ENSO: NOAA’s Oceanic Niño Index (ONI).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rain = pd.read_csv("cocoa_belt_chirps_monthly.csv", parse_dates=["month"]).set_index("month")["rain_mm"]

df = pd.DataFrame({"cocoa": cocoa, "rain": rain, "oni": oni}).dropna()
df["ret"] = np.log(df["cocoa"]).diff()

title: XGBoost 101: Cocoa, Weather and the Curve
section: 2. Weather features that make agronomic sense
text:
2. Weather features that make agronomic sense
Raw rainfall is less useful than anomalies against the normal for that calendar month, and cocoa cares about accumulated stress over several months:
clim = df.groupby(df.index.month)["rain"].transform("mean")
df["rain_anom"] = df["rain"] / clim - 1

X = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
X["rain_anom_1m"] = df["rain_anom"].shift(1)
X["rain_anom_3m"] = df["rain_anom"].rolling(3).mean().shift(1)
X["rain_anom_6m"] = df["rain_anom"].rolling(6).mean().shift(1)
X["oni_lag2"]     = df["oni"].shift(2)
X["mom_3m"]       = df["ret"].rolling(3).sum().shift(1)
X["mom_12m"]      = df["ret"].rolling(12).sum().shift(1)
X["month"]        = df.index.month          # main crop Oct–Mar, mid-crop Apr–Sep

y = (df["ret"].shift(-1) > 0).astype(int)
data = X.join(y.rename("up")).dropna()
Every feature is shifted so it is known before the month we predict.

title: XGBoost 101: Cocoa, Weather and the Curve
text:
3. Training XGBoost
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, accuracy_score

train = data.loc[:"2018-12"]
valid = data.loc["2019-01":"2021-12"]
test  = data.loc["2022-01":]

feat = [c for c in data.columns if c != "up"]
model = XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=1000, learning_rate=0.02, max_depth=2,
    subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, reg_lambda=1.0,
    eval_metric="auc", early_stopping_rounds=50,
)
model.fit(train[feat], train["up"], eval_set=[(valid[feat], valid["up"])], verbose=False)

p = model.predict_proba(test[feat])[:, 1]
print("Best iteration:", model.best_iteration)
print("Test AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(test["up"], p), 3))
print("Test accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(test["up"], p > 0.5), 3))
Early stopping on a separate validation period picks the number of trees for us and is the single most effective guard against overfitting with boosting.

title: XGBoost 101: Cocoa, Weather and the Curve
text:
4. Tuning
With only a few hundred monthly observations, keep the search small and the trees shallow:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, TimeSeriesSplit

grid = GridSearchCV(
    XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.03, eval_metric="auc"),
    {"max_depth": [1, 2, 3], "min_child_weight": [1, 5, 10], "subsample": [0.7, 1.0]},
    cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5), scoring="roc_auc",
)
grid.fit(pd.concat([train, valid])[feat], pd.concat([train, valid])["up"])
print(grid.best_params_)

title: XGBoost 101: Cocoa, Weather and the Curve
text:
5. Explaining the model with SHAP
SHAP values show how much each feature pushed each prediction up or down:
import shap
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
sv = explainer.shap_values(test[feat])
shap.summary_plot(sv, test[feat])
Look for whether dry anomalies (negative rain_anom_3m) push the probability of a rise up, as agronomy would suggest. If the model relies on the opposite sign, be suspicious.

title: XGBoost 101: Cocoa, Weather and the Curve
text:
6. Ablation: does weather add anything?
Retrain without the weather columns and compare:
base_feat = ["mom_3m", "mom_12m", "month"]
m0 = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=model.best_iteration + 1, learning_rate=0.02, max_depth=2,
                   subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8).fit(train[base_feat], train["up"])
print("AUC without weather:", round(roc_auc_score(test["up"], m0.predict_proba(test[base_feat])[:, 1]), 3))
On monthly data the difference is often small, and that is a fair conclusion. Weather is far more useful at higher resolution: daily rainfall and soil moisture by region, mapped to crop calendars, combined with field reports on pod counts and disease.

title: Forecasting Softs Prices with Time Series Methods (R and Python)
text:
1. Data
We use the World Bank Pink Sheet (CMO-Historical-Data-Monthly.xlsx), which has long monthly histories for Coffee, Arabica and Coffee, Robusta in US$/kg.

title: Forecasting Softs Prices with Time Series Methods (R and Python)
text:
2. Time series components
A monthly series can be split into:

Trend: the long-run level, driven by costs, demand growth and inflation.
Seasonality: recurring patterns within the year. Coffee prices have some, linked to harvest timing and frost risk in Brazil, but it is weak relative to price swings.
Remainder: everything else, which for commodities is most of the story: weather shocks, currency moves, logistics and positioning.

title: Forecasting Softs Prices with Time Series Methods (R and Python)
text:
3. Forecasting in R
library(readxl)
library(forecast)

wb <- read_excel("CMO-Historical-Data-Monthly.xlsx", sheet = "Monthly Prices", skip = 4)
names(wb)[1] <- "month"
wb <- wb[grepl("^\\d{4}M\\d{2}$", wb$month), ]

arabica <- ts(as.numeric(wb$`Coffee, Arabica`), start = c(1960, 1), frequency = 12)
arabica <- window(arabica, start = c(2000, 1))

plot(arabica, main = "Arabica coffee, US$/kg")

# Decompose the log series (multiplicative effects become additive)
dec <- stl(log(arabica), s.window = "periodic")
plot(dec)
The seasonal panel will be small compared with the remainder. That alone tells you seasonality will not drive the forecast.
Fit an ARIMA model automatically and forecast 12 months ahead:
fit <- auto.arima(log(arabica))
summary(fit)

fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12)
plot(fc, main = "12-month ARIMA forecast (log arabica)")
The widening fan is the most useful output: it shows how quickly uncertainty grows. Most automatically selected models for commodity prices end up close to a random walk.
Compare with the simplest possible benchmark, the naive forecast (next month equals this month), on a hold-out period:
train <- window(log(arabica), end = c(2019, 12))
test  <- window(log(arabica), start = c(2020, 1))

fit_tr <- auto.arima(train)
fc_ar  <- forecast(fit_tr, h = length(test))
fc_nv  <- naive(train, h = length(test))

accuracy(fc_ar, test)
accuracy(fc_nv, test)

title: Forecasting Softs Prices with Time Series Methods (R and Python)
text:
4. Forecasting in Python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

wb = pd.read_excel("CMO-Historical-Data-Monthly.xlsx", sheet_name="Monthly Prices", skiprows=4)
wb = wb.rename(columns={wb.columns[0]: "month"})
wb = wb[wb["month"].astype(str).str.match(r"^\d{4}M\d{2}$")]
wb.index = pd.to_datetime(wb["month"].str.replace("M", "-"), format="%Y-%m")
coffee = wb[["Coffee, Arabica", "Coffee, Robusta"]].astype(float).loc["2000":]
coffee.columns = ["arabica", "robusta"]

STL(np.log(coffee["robusta"]), period=12).fit().plot()
plt.show()
A rolling-origin evaluation is more honest than a single split: refit each month and forecast one step ahead.
y = np.log(coffee["robusta"])
preds, actual = [], []
for end in pd.date_range("2018-01-01", y.index[-2], freq="MS"):
    model = ARIMA(y.loc[:end], order=(1, 1, 0)).fit()
    preds.append(model.forecast(1).iloc[0])
    actual.append(y.shift(-1).loc[end])

preds, actual = np.array(preds), np.array(actual)
naive = y.loc["2018-01-01":y.index[-2]].values
print("ARIMA MAE:", np.mean(np.abs(preds - actual)).round(4))
print("Naive MAE:", np.mean(np.abs(naive - actual)).round(4))

title: Forecasting Softs Prices with Time Series Methods (R and Python)
text:
5. Prophet
Prophet handles trend changes and seasonality with little tuning:
from prophet import Prophet

d = coffee["arabica"].reset_index()
d.columns = ["ds", "y"]
d["y"] = np.log(d["y"])

m = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True, changepoint_prior_scale=0.3)
m.fit(d.loc[d["ds"] < "2023-01-01"])
future = m.make_future_dataframe(periods=24, freq="MS")
fc = m.predict(future)
m.plot(fc); m.plot_components(fc)
plt.show()
Prophet extrapolates the recent trend, so after a big rally it will tend to forecast more rally. Check its changepoints against what actually happened in the market.

title: Forecasting Softs Prices with Time Series Methods (R and Python)
section: 6. Modelling a spread instead of a level
text:
6. Modelling a spread instead of a level
Relative value is often more forecastable than outright price. The arabica–robusta spread reflects quality premia and the relative supply from Brazil, Colombia and Central America versus Vietnam, Brazil (conilon) and Uganda:
spread = coffee["arabica"] - coffee["robusta"]
spread.plot(title="Arabica minus robusta, US$/kg")
plt.axhline(spread.loc["2010":].mean(), ls="--", color="grey")
plt.show()

from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
print("ADF p-value (spread):", round(adfuller(spread.dropna())[1], 3))
A low p-value suggests the spread tends to revert to its mean. Mean-reversion is never guaranteed, but this is the kind of structure that univariate models can use.

title: Forecasting Softs Prices with Time Series Methods (R and Python)
text:
7. Takeaways

Price-only models rarely beat a naive forecast for softs outright prices. Use them as baselines.
Their real value is in quantifying uncertainty and in modelling more stable quantities: spreads, seasonal patterns and basis.
Forecasting supply shocks needs fundamental inputs: weather, crop surveys, exports and stocks.
