title: Deep Learning for Time Series: LSTM and CNN Forecasts for Cotton
text:
1. Why cotton and which drivers?
Cotton prices respond to:

The US dollar: the US is the largest exporter, so a stronger dollar makes US cotton dearer abroad.
Crude oil: polyester, cotton’s main substitute, is made from oil.
Other markets’ risk appetite: cotton often trades with broader commodity and equity sentiment, captured here by the S&P 500.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf

tickers = {"cotton": "CT=F", "dxy": "DX-Y.NYB", "crude": "CL=F", "spx": "^GSPC"}
raw = yf.download(list(tickers.values()), start="2005-01-01", end="2024-06-30", interval="1wk")["Close"]
raw = raw.rename(columns={v: k for k, v in tickers.items()}).dropna()
rets = np.log(raw).diff().dropna()

title: Deep Learning for Time Series: LSTM and CNN Forecasts for Cotton
text:
2. Turning series into supervised windows
Each sample is the previous 26 weeks of all four return series; the target is next week’s cotton return.
def make_windows(df, target_col, lookback=26):
    values = df.values
    t_idx = df.columns.get_loc(target_col)
    X, y = [], []
    for i in range(lookback, len(df)):
        X.append(values[i - lookback:i])   # weeks i-lookback ... i-1
        y.append(values[i, t_idx])         # week i, the one after the window
    return np.array(X), np.array(y)
The window covers weeks i-26 to i-1 and the target is week i, the week immediately after it. Checking this indexing is worth five minutes, because an off-by-one error here produces a “perfect” model that is just reading the answer.
X, y = make_windows(rets, "cotton", lookback=26)
dates = rets.index[26:]   # date of each target week

train = dates < "2018-01-01"
valid = (dates >= "2018-01-01") & (dates < "2021-01-01")
test  = dates >= "2021-01-01"

# Scale using training statistics only
mu = X[train].reshape(-1, X.shape[2]).mean(0)
sd = X[train].reshape(-1, X.shape[2]).std(0)
X = (X - mu) / sd
y_scale = y[train].std()
y_s = y / y_scale

title: Deep Learning for Time Series: LSTM and CNN Forecasts for Cotton
text:
3. An LSTM model
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers

def build_lstm(n_steps, n_feat):
    model = keras.Sequential([
        layers.Input(shape=(n_steps, n_feat)),
        layers.LSTM(32),
        layers.Dropout(0.3),
        layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(1),
    ])
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), loss="mae")
    return model

lstm = build_lstm(X.shape[1], X.shape[2])
stop = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=20, restore_best_weights=True)
hist = lstm.fit(X[train], y_s[train], validation_data=(X[valid], y_s[valid]),
                epochs=300, batch_size=32, callbacks=[stop], verbose=0)
print("Stopped after", len(hist.history["loss"]), "epochs")
Small networks, dropout and early stopping are not optional with a few hundred weekly samples.

title: Deep Learning for Time Series: LSTM and CNN Forecasts for Cotton
text:
4. A 1D convolutional model
CNNs scan the window with filters that detect short patterns (for example, a sharp dollar move followed by cotton weakness):
def build_cnn(n_steps, n_feat):
    model = keras.Sequential([
        layers.Input(shape=(n_steps, n_feat)),
        layers.Conv1D(16, kernel_size=4, activation="relu"),
        layers.MaxPooling1D(2),
        layers.Conv1D(16, kernel_size=4, activation="relu"),
        layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D(),
        layers.Dropout(0.3),
        layers.Dense(1),
    ])
    model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mae")
    return model

cnn = build_cnn(X.shape[1], X.shape[2])
cnn.fit(X[train], y_s[train], validation_data=(X[valid], y_s[valid]),
        epochs=300, batch_size=32, callbacks=[stop], verbose=0)

title: Deep Learning for Time Series: LSTM and CNN Forecasts for Cotton
text:
5. Honest evaluation
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

def report(name, pred):
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y[test], pred)
    hit = (np.sign(pred) == np.sign(y[test])).mean()
    print(f"{name:8s} MAE={mae:.4f}  hit rate={hit:.3f}")

report("Zero", np.zeros(test.sum()))
ridge = Ridge(alpha=10).fit(X[train].reshape(train.sum(), -1), y[train])
report("Ridge", ridge.predict(X[test].reshape(test.sum(), -1)))
report("LSTM", lstm.predict(X[test], verbose=0).ravel() * y_scale)
report("CNN", cnn.predict(X[test], verbose=0).ravel() * y_scale)
Run the networks with several random seeds. If results swing with the seed, you are looking at noise, not skill.

title: Deep Learning for Time Series: LSTM and CNN Forecasts for Cotton
section: 6. Where deep learning does help in softs
text:
6. Where deep learning does help in softs
Weekly returns are close to unpredictable, so do not be surprised if the zero forecast is hard to beat. Neural networks earn their keep in richer problems:

Crop yield from sequences of daily weather and satellite vegetation indices over a season.
Physical flows: forecasting port arrivals or shipments from historical patterns and weather.
Text: classifying crop reports, weather bulletins or news by sentiment.
Images: detecting crop disease or land use, covered in Image classification.

title: Deep Learning for Time Series: LSTM and CNN Forecasts for Cotton
text:

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
text:
1. The data
Two open datasets on Mendeley Data work well:

RoCoLe (Robusta Coffee Leaf images, Ecuador): healthy leaves, red spider mite and rust at several severity levels.
JMuBEN (arabica leaves, Kenya): healthy leaves, leaf rust, Cercospora and Phoma.

Download one and arrange the images in one folder per class:
coffee_leaves/
    healthy/
    rust/
    cercospora/
    phoma/

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
text:
2. How CNNs see an image
A CNN slides small filters across the image. Early layers detect edges and colours; deeper layers combine them into textures and shapes, such as the orange powdery spots of rust or the brown rings of Cercospora. Pooling layers shrink the image so later layers see larger areas.
Training a CNN from scratch needs a lot of images. Transfer learning starts from a network already trained on millions of everyday photos (ImageNet) and only retrains the top layers, which works well with a few thousand leaves.

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
text:
3. Loading the images
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras
from tensorflow.keras import layers

IMG = (224, 224)
train_ds = keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory(
    "coffee_leaves", validation_split=0.2, subset="training", seed=42,
    image_size=IMG, batch_size=32)
val_ds = keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory(
    "coffee_leaves", validation_split=0.2, subset="validation", seed=42,
    image_size=IMG, batch_size=32)

class_names = train_ds.class_names
print(class_names)

AUTOTUNE = tf.data.AUTOTUNE
train_ds = train_ds.cache().shuffle(1000).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)
val_ds = val_ds.cache().prefetch(AUTOTUNE)
Check the class balance. Disease datasets are often dominated by healthy leaves, and a model that always says “healthy” can look accurate while being useless.

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
text:
4. Building the model
augment = keras.Sequential([
    layers.RandomFlip("horizontal_and_vertical"),
    layers.RandomRotation(0.2),
    layers.RandomZoom(0.15),
    layers.RandomContrast(0.2),
])

base = keras.applications.EfficientNetB0(include_top=False, weights="imagenet",
                                         input_shape=IMG + (3,))
base.trainable = False   # freeze the pretrained layers at first

inputs = keras.Input(shape=IMG + (3,))
x = augment(inputs)
x = keras.applications.efficientnet.preprocess_input(x)
x = base(x, training=False)
x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(len(class_names), activation="softmax")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3),
              loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
Augmentation imitates real field photos: leaves at different angles, lighting and distances.

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
text:
5. Training in two stages
stop = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)
model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, epochs=20, callbacks=[stop])

# Fine-tune: unfreeze the top of the base network with a small learning rate
base.trainable = True
for layer in base.layers[:-30]:
    layer.trainable = False
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-5),
              loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, epochs=10, callbacks=[stop])

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
text:
6. Evaluating properly
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix

y_true = np.concatenate([y.numpy() for _, y in val_ds])
y_pred = np.argmax(model.predict(val_ds), axis=1)

print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred, target_names=class_names))
print(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred))
Focus on recall for the disease classes: a missed rust case costs much more than a false alarm. If photos of the same tree or farm appear in both training and validation sets, accuracy will be inflated; split by farm or date where the metadata allows.

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
section: 7. From a classifier to market information
text:
7. From a classifier to market information
A leaf classifier on its own does not move prices. Its value comes when it is aggregated:

Field surveys: counting the share of diseased leaves across sampled farms gives an early, quantitative read on crop health, ahead of official estimates.
Satellite and drone imagery: the same CNN approach, applied to canopy images, maps stressed or dying plantations at scale. The Google Earth Engine tutorial covers vegetation indices from satellites.
Yield models: disease prevalence can be added as a feature alongside weather in crop forecasts.

title: Image Classification with Deep Learning: Detecting Coffee Leaf Disease
text:

Reinforcement learning moves from prediction to decision-making.

title: Reinforcement Learning 101: Q-Learning on Sugar Market Regimes
text:
1. The building blocks

Agent: the decision-maker (our trading rule).
Environment: the market, replayed from history.
State: what the agent observes, here the market regime.
Action: short, flat or long one unit of sugar.
Reward: the profit or loss from the position over the next week, minus transaction costs.

The agent learns a Q-table: for each state and action, the expected discounted future reward. It updates the table after every step with the Bellman equation:
\[
Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha \left[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a) \right]
\]
where α is the learning rate and γ the discount factor.

title: Reinforcement Learning 101: Q-Learning on Sugar Market Regimes
text:
2. Defining states from market regimes
Tabular Q-learning needs a small, discrete set of states. We describe each week by two features, each split into buckets:

Trend: 13-week return in three buckets (down, sideways, up).
Volatility: 13-week realised volatility in two buckets (calm, stressed).
Current position: short, flat or long, so the agent can account for trading costs.

That gives 3 × 2 × 3 = 18 states.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf

px = yf.download("SB=F", start="2008-01-01", end="2024-06-30", interval="1wk")["Close"].squeeze()
ret = np.log(px).diff()

trend = ret.rolling(13).sum()
vol = ret.rolling(13).std()

df = pd.DataFrame({"ret_next": ret.shift(-1), "trend": trend, "vol": vol}).dropna()
train = df.loc[:"2018-12"].copy()
test = df.loc["2019-01":].copy()

# Bucket edges from the training period only
t_edges = train["trend"].quantile([1/3, 2/3]).values
v_edge = train["vol"].median()

for d in (train, test):
    d["t_bin"] = np.digitize(d["trend"], t_edges)        # 0, 1, 2
    d["v_bin"] = (d["vol"] > v_edge).astype(int)         # 0, 1

text:
4. Training the agent
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Q = np.zeros((18, 3))
alpha, gamma = 0.05, 0.9
epsilon, eps_min, eps_decay = 1.0, 0.05, 0.995

rows = list(train.itertuples())
for episode in range(500):
    pos = 0
    for i in range(len(rows) - 1):
        s = state_id(rows[i].t_bin, rows[i].v_bin, pos)
        a = rng.integers(3) if rng.random() < epsilon else int(Q[s].argmax())
        pos, r = step(rows[i], pos, a)
        s_next = state_id(rows[i + 1].t_bin, rows[i + 1].v_bin, pos)
        Q[s, a] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q[s_next].max() - Q[s, a])
    epsilon = max(eps_min, epsilon * eps_decay)
The ε-greedy rule makes the agent explore random actions early on, then increasingly exploit what it has learned.

title: Reinforcement Learning 101: Q-Learning on Sugar Market Regimes
text:
5. Reading the learned policy
labels = ["short", "flat", "long"]
policy = []
for t in range(3):
    for v in range(2):
        s = state_id(t, v, 0)
        policy.append({"trend": ["down", "sideways", "up"][t],
                       "vol": ["calm", "stressed"][v],
                       "action_from_flat": labels[int(Q[s].argmax())]})
pd.DataFrame(policy)
If the agent has learned something like “long in calm up-trends, flat in stressed markets”, it has rediscovered a trend-following rule with a volatility filter. That is a good sign the machinery works, and a reminder that RL often finds familiar strategies.

title: Reinforcement Learning 101: Q-Learning on Sugar Market Regimes
text:
6. Testing on unseen years
pos, pnl = 0, []
for row in test.itertuples():
    s = state_id(row.t_bin, row.v_bin, pos)
    pos, r = step(row, pos, int(Q[s].argmax()))
    pnl.append(r)

pnl = pd.Series(pnl, index=test.index)
print("Test cumulative log return:", round(pnl.sum(), 3))
print("Buy and hold:", round(test["ret_next"].sum(), 3))
print("Weekly Sharpe (annualised):", round(np.sqrt(52) * pnl.mean() / pnl.std(), 2))

text:
7. Limits of tabular Q-learning

Few states: real markets need far richer descriptions (curve shape, positioning, weather), which explode the table size.
One history: the agent sees each historical path many times and can memorise it. Out-of-sample testing is essential.
No market impact: we assume we can trade at the close with a fixed cost.

The next tutorial replaces the table with a neural network.

2. Features for the agent
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf

px = yf.download("CC=F", start="2010-01-01", end="2024-06-30")["Close"].squeeze()
ret = np.log(px).diff()

feat = pd.DataFrame({
    "ret_1d": ret,
    "ret_5d": ret.rolling(5).sum(),
    "ret_20d": ret.rolling(20).sum(),
    "ret_60d": ret.rolling(60).sum(),
    "vol_20d": ret.rolling(20).std(),
    "dist_ma100": px / px.rolling(100).mean() - 1,
}).dropna()
next_ret = ret.shift(-1).reindex(feat.index)

train_idx = feat.index < "2019-01-01"
mu, sd = feat[train_idx].mean(), feat[train_idx].std()
feat_z = ((feat - mu) / sd).clip(-5, 5)    # scale with training statistics only
A note on data: CC=F is a continuous front-month series that jumps at each contract roll. For research beyond a tutorial, build a roll-adjusted series from individual contract months.

title: RL and Trading in Futures Markets 101: A Deep Q-Network for Cocoa
text:
3. The trading environment
The agent chooses short, flat or long each day. The reward is the next day’s return on the chosen position, minus a cost whenever the position changes. The current position is part of the observation so the agent can weigh trading costs.
import gymnasium as gym
from gymnasium import spaces

class FuturesEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self, features, next_returns, cost=0.0005, episode_len=250):
        super().__init__()
        self.X = features.values.astype(np.float32)
        self.r = next_returns.values.astype(np.float32)
        self.cost, self.episode_len = cost, episode_len
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(3)        # 0 short, 1 flat, 2 long
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(-np.inf, np.inf, shape=(self.X.shape[1] + 1,), dtype=np.float32)

    def _obs(self):
        return np.append(self.X[self.t], self.pos).astype(np.float32)

    def reset(self, seed=None, options=None):
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self.t = self.np_random.integers(0, len(self.X) - self.episode_len - 1)
        self.end = self.t + self.episode_len
        self.pos = 0.0
        return self._obs(), {}

    def step(self, action):
        new_pos = float(action) - 1.0
        reward = new_pos * self.r[self.t] - self.cost * abs(new_pos - self.pos)
        self.pos = new_pos
        self.t += 1
        terminated = self.t >= self.end
        return self._obs(), float(reward), terminated, False, {}
Each episode is a random one-year slice of history, which gives the agent many different market conditions to learn from.

title: RL and Trading in Futures Markets 101: A Deep Q-Network for Cocoa
text:
4. Training the DQN
from stable_baselines3 import DQN

train_env = FuturesEnv(feat_z[train_idx], next_ret[train_idx])

model = DQN(
    "MlpPolicy", train_env,
    learning_rate=1e-4, buffer_size=50_000, batch_size=64,
    gamma=0.95, exploration_fraction=0.3, exploration_final_eps=0.05,
    policy_kwargs={"net_arch": [64, 64]}, seed=0, verbose=0,
)
model.learn(total_timesteps=200_000)
The key DQN ideas are all inside stable-baselines3:

Experience replay: past transitions are stored in a buffer and sampled at random, which breaks the correlation between consecutive days.
Target network: a slowly updated copy of the network provides stable learning targets.
ε-greedy exploration: the agent acts randomly at first and gradually relies on its learned values.

title: RL and Trading in Futures Markets 101: A Deep Q-Network for Cocoa
text:
5. Out-of-sample evaluation
test_X = feat_z[~train_idx]
test_r = next_ret[~train_idx].fillna(0)

pos, pnl, positions = 0.0, [], []
for i in range(len(test_X)):
    obs = np.append(test_X.values[i], pos).astype(np.float32)
    action, _ = model.predict(obs, deterministic=True)
    new_pos = float(action) - 1.0
    pnl.append(new_pos * test_r.values[i] - 0.0005 * abs(new_pos - pos))
    pos = new_pos
    positions.append(pos)

pnl = pd.Series(pnl, index=test_X.index)
print("Cumulative log return:", round(pnl.sum(), 3))
print("Buy and hold:", round(test_r.sum(), 3))
print("Annualised Sharpe:", round(np.sqrt(252) * pnl.mean() / pnl.std(), 2))
print("Share of days long / flat / short:",
      pd.Series(positions).value_counts(normalize=True).round(2).to_dict())
Check performance separately for 2019–2022 and for 2023–24. If the agent made most of its money in the 2024 rally simply by being long, it has learned “cocoa goes up”, not a robust strategy.

title: RL and Trading in Futures Markets 101: A Deep Q-Network for Cocoa
text:
6. Making it more realistic
Before trusting any RL trading result, add:

Proper contracts and rolls rather than a continuous series.
Realistic costs: exchange fees, bid-ask spreads and slippage, which widen sharply in volatile markets such as 2024 cocoa.
Position sizing and risk limits: scale positions by volatility and cap drawdowns.
Walk-forward training: retrain on an expanding window and test on the following period, repeatedly.
Multiple seeds: RL results vary a lot between runs; report the spread, not the best run.
